lessons.title: The NFL in one picture
lessons.lead: Thirty-two teams. Two conference races. One Super Bowl. Your fantasy roster cuts across all of them.

sections.title: Know which race you are watching
sections.text: The AFC and NFC each contain 16 teams, divided into four divisions of four. A club plays 17 regular-season games across 18 weeks; its bye is the week it does not play.

sections.title: Why a division game has extra weight
sections.text: Each team faces its three division rivals twice. Division winners claim four playoff places per conference; three more go to wild cards. Only the No. 1 seed in each conference skips the Wild Card round. That is why standings, division results and home-field advantage matter even when a fantasy star has a big afternoon.

question.prompt: Can two teams from the same division reach the playoffs?
options: Yes: a division winner and a wild card can both qualify.
No: one playoff team per division.
Only if both win the division.
feedback: Correct. Wild-card places let additional teams from a division qualify.
A division title guarantees a place, but wild cards create additional paths.
A tied record is settled by tiebreakers; a second team can still enter as a wild card.

lessons.title: Read the situation before the highlight
lessons.lead: A five-yard gain can be a strong first-down play and a failed third-down play. The scoreboard strip tells you which.

sections.title: Translate the TV graphic
sections.text: Third-and-7 means this is the offense’s third down and it needs seven yards to earn a new series. The usual new series starts first-and-10; near the goal line it can be goal-to-go.

sections.title: Make the result mean something
sections.text: On first-and-10, five yards leaves second-and-5. On third-and-7, the same gain leaves fourth-and-2. The second play produced yards without earning another first down. Score, remaining time and field position shape whether the next call is a punt, field goal or attempt to convert.

lessons.title: Find the work before chasing the points
lessons.lead: Carries, routes and targets describe opportunity. Catches, yards and touchdowns tell you what happened with it.

sections.title: Follow one play through the offense
sections.text: A running back can carry the ball, catch a pass, run a route without being targeted, or stay in to block. A receiver can be on the field yet never receive the throw. Being present is different from being involved.

sections.title: Ask the next useful question
sections.text: For a back: how many carries and receptions, and who handles scoring chances? For a pass catcher: how often does he run a route, get targeted and convert those throws? A teammate’s absence can create chances, but it does not guarantee one replacement inherits all of them.

lessons.title: A great average needs a workload
lessons.lead: Yards per carry answers how efficient the runs were in aggregate. It does not tell you how many chances the back received.

sections.title: Keep both numbers on the screen
sections.text: A hypothetical runner with 80 yards on 20 carries averages 4.0 yards per carry. Another with 48 yards on six carries averages 8.0. The second runner was more efficient in that sample; the first accumulated more rushing yards.

sections.title: Then look inside the average
sections.text: Five five-yard runs and a sequence of −2, 0, 2, 5 and 20 yards both total 25 yards on five carries: 5.0 yards per carry. The paths look very different on third down. An average is not a promise that each future run gains that amount.

question.prompt: Which statement is justified by 48 yards on six carries?
options: The back will gain eight yards on every carry.
He averaged eight yards per carry in that six-carry sample.
He had more rushing yards than a back with 80.
feedback: The average combines the whole sample, including short gains and explosive plays.
Correct. Keep the period and sample size attached to the number.
Efficiency and total production are different: 48 is less than 80.

lessons.title: Your league changes what a catch is worth
lessons.lead: The same NFL stat line can score differently in standard, half-PPR, full-PPR and tight-end-premium formats.

sections.title: Separate the scoring ingredients
sections.text: In this teaching example, receiving yards score 0.1 points each and a receiving touchdown scores six. A player with six catches for 60 yards and no touchdown earns six yardage points. Reception scoring then adds zero, three or six points.

sections.title: A premium is an extra rule, not a universal rate
sections.text: With full PPR plus an extra 0.5 points for each tight end reception, that same TE scores 15: six from yards, six from normal receptions and three from the premium. Your league’s saved rules decide the real number; a provider’s default is not proof of your commissioner’s settings.

question.prompt: Why can a six-catch tight end score more than a six-catch receiver with identical yards and TDs?
options: Tight ends always receive more points in fantasy.
This league may award an extra reception bonus to tight ends.
Targets always count as catches.
feedback: Only the league’s scoring settings can create that difference.
Correct. Positional reception bonuses are configurable; verify the actual rate.
An incomplete target is not a reception.

lessons.title: The best option must fit the slot and the clock
lessons.lead: Superflex changes who you can start. Game times change how long you have to decide.

sections.title: Start with legal choices
sections.text: A standard Sleeper FLEX accepts RB, WR or TE. Super Flex can also accept a quarterback. In a hypothetical Superflex decision, a QB projected for 20 and a WR projected for 13 can compete for the same spot; the QB cannot fill an ordinary FLEX. Projections are estimates, not points already earned.

sections.title: Protect the decision you still have
sections.text: A Monday player gives you less replacement flexibility once Sunday alternatives have started. Check the actual platform lock state, eligibility and injury report before making a change. Sleeper AutoSub pairs can lock both players as soon as either player kicks off, so kickoff alone may not describe the whole restriction.

feedback: Once the alternative locks, it usually cannot be newly inserted. Check the platform and any AutoSub exception before relying on it.

stories.title: Buffalo’s fast start has two sides
stories.lead: Allen’s five touchdowns drove a Thursday win; DJ Moore’s injury is the next thing to follow.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Buffalo beat Detroit 41–31 on September 17. Josh Allen threw for 248 yards and three touchdowns and ran for 69 yards and two more scores. DJ Moore left in the second quarter and was ruled out for the remainder of that game with a shoulder/stinger injury.

sections.title: Why fans care
sections.text: Quarterback rushing can drive both real scoring and fantasy production. The important follow-up for Moore managers is his next availability update, because Thursday’s Week 2 score is already in the books.

sections.title: Separate a finished game from the next decision
sections.text: An OUT label can describe an in-game exit. It does not establish that a player can still be swapped this week or that he is ruled out next week.

question.prompt: DJ Moore’s Thursday OUT tag proves what?
options: He was ruled out for the rest of that Thursday game.
He is officially out for Week 3.
You can replace his Week 2 score on Sunday.
feedback: Correct. The cited announcement is tied to the September 17 game.
The source did not establish next week’s availability.
The game has finished; check your league’s locked score rather than assuming a swap is possible.

stories.title: Kenneth Walker gives Kansas City another way to win
stories.lead: Start with the 23 carries. Then appreciate the 7.5 yards per carry.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Kansas City opened with a 31–10 win over Denver. Walker’s Chiefs debut included 173 rushing yards on 23 attempts plus three catches for 18 yards, with a rushing touchdown and a receiving touchdown. The official table also gives Kelce three catches for 71 yards.

sections.title: Why fans care
sections.text: This was efficiency attached to a substantial workload. The Colts matchup gives you another chance to see whether that role persists when the game develops differently.

sections.title: Volume plus efficiency
sections.text: One explosive opening game is evidence of a ceiling, not a season-long average. Keep carries, receptions and scoring chances beside the yards-per-carry figure.

question.prompt: Which fact best explains why this was more than one long run?
options: Walker had 26 total touches.
A 7.5 average means every run gained 7.5.
One game guarantees the same role all season.
feedback: Correct. His 23 carries and 3 catches describe meaningful opportunity.
The average combines all 23 runs.
Future workload remains something to observe.

stories.title: Seattle changes quarterbacks, so watch the whole offense
stories.lead: Drew Lock starts at Arizona with Sam Darnold ruled out.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Seattle confirmed Darnold will miss Week 2 with a glute injury and Lock will start. In relief during the opener, Lock completed 16 of 22 passes for 187 yards and a touchdown. His full week with the starters is relevant preparation; it is not proof Sunday will repeat that performance.

sections.title: Why fans care
sections.text: For a Smith-Njigba manager, the useful question is how the new quarterback changes target distribution and drive quality. For a Superflex manager, a named NFL starter creates a different option than a backup who may never enter.

sections.title: Quarterback context travels to teammates
sections.text: Watch where the throws go and how often drives stay alive. A quarterback change should trigger a fresh read of the offense, not an automatic upgrade or downgrade for every receiver.

question.prompt: What would most directly show how the QB change affected Smith-Njigba?
options: His actual routes and targets with Lock.
Lock’s jersey number.
Assuming every backup targets the same receiver.
feedback: Correct. Look for observed involvement in this offense.
That tells you who is playing, not how opportunities are distributed.
The distribution has to be observed.

stories.title: Carson Wentz gets the call in an NFC North game
stories.lead: Kyler Murray is out; Minnesota takes a different quarterback into Chicago.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: The Vikings announced Wentz will start against the Bears after Murray was ruled out following his Week 1 concussion. Wentz’s relief appearance against Green Bay produced 133 passing yards and three touchdowns on 12 completions in 19 attempts. Sunday will be his 100th career start.

sections.title: Why fans care
sections.text: Jefferson’s talent is familiar; his next game’s quarterback and game flow are different inputs. Three touchdown passes on 19 attempts also illustrate how scoring can make a small sample look enormous.

sections.title: Touchdowns and sample size
sections.text: Do not turn one efficient relief appearance into a new weekly expectation. Follow the sustained passing workload, accuracy and scoring chances against the next defense.

question.prompt: Does three TDs on 19 attempts establish Wentz’s normal TD rate?
options: Yes, it is now his weekly baseline.
No, it is one short sample with a new opponent next.
Only passing yards matter.
feedback: A small sample can be driven by a few scoring plays.
Correct. Recognize the performance while keeping uncertainty about repeatability.
Touchdowns matter, but they need context alongside workload and efficiency.

stories.title: Puka Nacua’s Monday status puts the clock in play
stories.lead: Questionable on the final report is still a decision waiting for more information.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: The Rams listed Nacua questionable for Monday night against the Giants with a hip injury. The team described soreness around his groin and said his playing status remained undetermined. Jordan Whittington was doubtful, adding uncertainty to Los Angeles’ receiving group.

sections.title: Why fans care
sections.text: Even if Nacua is not on your roster, this is a useful case for any late-playing questionable starter. Waiting has value only if you still have an eligible alternative when the answer arrives.

sections.title: The fallback has a deadline too
sections.text: Separate the probability of playing from the ability to react. Identify the replacement and its effective lock before Sunday alternatives begin.

Eligibility, ownership and deadlines are part of the decision.

stories.title: Houston has to replace Nico Collins’ opportunity
stories.lead: The formal OUT designation is clear; the destination of his targets is not.

sections.text: Collins was ruled out of Sunday’s Bengals game with a hamstring injury. His Week 1 line was seven catches on 10 targets for 75 yards and a touchdown. Houston now has to distribute that work differently; one absent player’s targets are not automatically handed to one replacement.

sections.title: Why fans care
sections.text: This directly affects Collins managers and changes the offensive context around Montgomery and Stroud. It is also a source-reading lesson: Cincinnati’s official report and team writer list Burrow questionable despite conflicting NFL.com copy saying no designation.

Collins is ruled out; the distribution among teammates remains uncertain.
Houston must stop throwing.
feedback: Target totals are not reserved slots that move intact to one teammate.
Correct. Availability is known; role redistribution is still an inference.
The offense can change its mix and distribute passes among multiple players.

stories.title: Derrick Henry’s milestone came with a full workload
stories.lead: A historic touchdown count is the headline. The 24 carries explain the afternoon.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Baltimore beat Indianapolis 41–23 behind 144 rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns from Henry. His career rushing-touchdown total reached 125, moving him past Marcus Allen into third all-time. The Ravens produced 506 offensive yards in the opener.

sections.title: Why fans care
sections.text: Fans recognize the career milestone; fantasy managers should also notice sustained opportunity. Three rushing touchdowns can swing a matchup, but they are not a sensible guarantee for the next game.

sections.title: Honor the ceiling; inspect the repeatable work
sections.text: Watch carries, scoring-area usage and how the offense sustains drives. Those help interpret a huge score without simply projecting three touchdowns forward.

question.prompt: Which is the clearest workload fact from this game?
options: Henry had 24 carries.
He is guaranteed three TDs next week.
Every carry gained six yards.
feedback: Correct. Carries describe the actual number of rushing opportunities.
Scoring outcomes vary; one game cannot guarantee the next.
Six was the aggregate average, not every result.
